gloss: strike; strike dead, kill; defeat; blow, wound, plague, slaughter
summary: The root is to strike: to land a blow on a person, a beast or a thing. The verb is used almost only in the hiphil, הִכָּה, and what the blow does is told by the context: a man is beaten and lives (Exo 21:18–19), or is struck and dies (Exo 21:12), an army or a city is struck “to the mouth of the sword” and so defeated and slain (Jos 10:28), and Yahweh strikes Egypt, Israel and the nations with plague, disease, blindness and the sword, both to judge and to correct (Exo 12:29; Deu 28:22; Jer 2:30). The noun מַכָּה is the blow and what it leaves: a stroke of the rod, a wound, a plague, a slaughter. Scripture uses the root of the Messiah: “struck of God” in men's eyes (Isa 53:4), the shepherd whom Yahweh's sword strikes (Zec 13:7; Mat 26:31), and the one who will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth (Isa 11:4; Rev 19:15). Arabic نِكَايَة, slaying and wounding among an enemy, and Aramaic נְכֵי, to harm, be injured, are the same root.

words.gloss: strike; strike dead; defeat; (of God) strike with plague or judgment
words.summary: About five hundred times, all but a handful in the hiphil (הִכָּה, imperfect יַכֶּה, shortened וַיַּךְ, imperative הַךְ, participle מַכֶּה), with the hophal as its passive; the qal is not found. The first letter נ is lost in most forms, so the root shows chiefly as a doubled כ. The verb names the blow, not its result: the same word is a slap on the cheek, a flogging, a killing, the rout of an army and the plagues of Egypt, and the context or an added “and he died” says which.

stems.gloss: strike, beat; strike dead, kill; strike down, defeat (an enemy, a city); (of God) strike with plague, disease, judgment; strike a thing; clap (the hands)

senses.gloss: strike, hit, beat (a blow that does not kill)
senses.definition: To land a blow or blows on a person or a beast with the hand, a fist, a stone, a rod or a whip: to hit, slap, beat or flog. The one struck lives; the law treats such a blow apart from one that kills, and limits a judicial beating to forty.

evidence.note: “A man strikes (וְהִכָּה) his neighbour with a stone or with a fist, and he does not die but falls to his bed”: if he rises again, הַמַּכֶּה, the striker, is clear, and pays for the lost time and the healing.

The guilty man who is בִּן הַכּוֹת, “a son of striking”, is beaten before the judge by number: “forty he shall strike him (יַכֶּנּוּ), he shall not add”, lest with מַכָּה רַבָּה, many blows more, “your brother be made light of before your eyes”.
Moses “saw an Egyptian man מַכֶּה a Hebrew man of his brothers”.
To the Hebrew in the wrong: “Why do you strike (תַכֶּה) your neighbour?”
The donkey to Balaam: “What have I done to you, that you have struck me (הִכִּיתַנִי) these three times?” (Num 22:23, 25, 27, with the staff).
Zedekiah “struck Micaiah on the cheek”.
“When you strike him (תַכֶּנּוּ) with the rod he will not die. You shall strike him with the rod, and deliver his soul from the grave”: the blow that corrects is set against death.
A rebuke goes deeper into a man of understanding “than striking (מֵהַכּוֹת) a fool a hundred times”.
A man who strikes his servant's eye and destroys it lets him go free for his eye.
The watchmen “struck me, they wounded me”.
Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and put him in the stocks; so the princes in Jer 37:15.
Nehemiah contended with the men who had married foreign wives, “and struck some of them and pulled out their hair”.
Yahweh's servant: “My back I gave to strikers (לְמַכִּים) and my cheeks to those who pluck; my face I did not hide from shame and spitting.”
“Let him give his cheek to the one striking him (לְמַכֵּהוּ).”
“With the rod they strike (יַכּוּ) on the cheek the judge of Israel”: the next verse names the ruler who comes out of Bethlehem.
They spat in his face and struck him, saying “Prophesy to us, Christ, who is it that struck you?”: Isa 50:6 done to Jesus.
The soldiers took the reed and struck him on the head: the rod of Mic 4:14.
“Whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also”: Lam 3:30 and Isa 50:6 made a command.

senses.gloss: strike dead, kill (a man, a beast)
senses.definition: To strike so that the one struck dies: to kill a man or a beast, by murder, by accident, in a fight or by an executioner. The verb is often followed by “and he died” or “and he put him to death”, and the law's word for the one who does it is רֹצֵחַ, a manslayer. Its object is often a נֶפֶשׁ, a soul.

evidence.note: “מַכֵּה אִישׁ וָמֵת: one who strikes a man and he dies shall surely be put to death.”
“If he struck him (הִכָּהוּ) with a tool of iron and he died, he is a manslayer (רֹצֵחַ)”; so with a stone, a wooden tool, or the hand in enmity (Num 35:17–21).
“A man who strikes (יַכֶּה) any soul of man shall surely be put to death; and one who strikes the soul of a beast (מַכֵּה נֶפֶשׁ־בְּהֵמָה) shall make it good, soul for soul.”
The sign set for Cain, “so that anyone finding him should not strike him (הַכּוֹת אֹתוֹ)”, answers “whoever kills (הֹרֵג) Cain”.
Reuben: “לֹא נַכֶּנּוּ נָפֶשׁ, let us not strike him, a soul”, that is, take his life.

Moses “struck (וַיַּךְ) the Egyptian and hid him in the sand”; Stephen says he “avenged the oppressed one, striking the Egyptian” (Act 7:24), and the Hebrew next day, “do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” (Exo 2:14).
The manslayer “who strikes his neighbour without knowing”; the avenger of blood may overtake him “and strike him, a soul (וְהִכָּהוּ נָפֶשׁ)”.
The cities of refuge are for “a manslayer, מַכֵּה־נֶפֶשׁ by mistake”; Num 35:15, 30; Jos 20:3.
“Cursed is he who strikes his neighbour in secret.”
A slain man found in the field, “and it is not known who struck him”.
David of the lion and the bear: “I went out after it and struck it … I seized its beard and struck it and killed it (וַהֲמִיתִּיו).”
The stone “struck the Philistine on his forehead”; David “struck the Philistine and put him to death”.
Abner struck Asahel in the belly with the butt of the spear, “and he fell there and died”.
Nathan to David: “Uriah the Hittite you have struck with the sword.”
Shallum conspired against Zechariah, “and struck him before the people and put him to death, and reigned in his place”: the usual word for the killing of a king (1Ki 15:27; 16:10; 2Ki 15:14, 25, 30).
Jehoiakim “struck him with the sword” and threw Uriah's body among the graves of the people.
“The king of Babylon struck them and put them to death at Riblah.”

senses.gloss: strike down, defeat, slaughter (an enemy, an army, a city, a land)
senses.definition: In war: to strike a king, a people, an army, a camp or a city, that is, to defeat it with slaughter. The phrase לְפִי־חֶרֶב, “to the mouth of the sword”, says that those struck were killed; a number of the slain or a pursuit often follows.

evidence.note: Joshua took Makkedah “and struck it and its king to the mouth of the sword; he devoted them and every soul in it; he left no survivor”.
“They struck every soul that was in it to the mouth of the sword, devoting them; nothing that breathed was left.”
Yahweh threw them into panic before Israel, “and struck them a great striking (וַיַּכֵּם מַכָּה־גְדוֹלָה) at Gibeon, and pursued them … and struck them as far as Azekah”: the verb with its own noun.
Chedorlaomer and the kings with him “struck the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim”: the verb's first use of war; Abram in turn struck them and pursued them (Gen 14:15).
Jacob fears that Esau “will come and strike me, mother with children”.
“Israel struck him to the mouth of the sword and took possession of his land”: Sihon.
The city turned to other gods: “striking you shall strike (הַכֵּה תַכֶּה) the inhabitants of that city to the mouth of the sword.”
“These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the sons of Israel struck.”
Shamgar “struck the Philistines, six hundred men, with an ox goad”.
Samson with the jawbone of a donkey “struck a thousand men”.
“Jonathan struck the garrison of the Philistines that was in Geba.”
The women's song: “Saul has struck (הִכָּה) his thousands, and David his ten thousands.”
“David struck the Philistines and subdued them.”
Israel rose “and struck Moab, and they fled before them”.
The army of Pharaoh Neco at Carchemish, “which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon struck”.
Yahweh “struck many nations and killed mighty kings”; so Psa 136:17.

senses.gloss: (of God) strike with plague, disease, blindness, death, judgment
senses.definition: Yahweh, or his angel, strikes a man, a people or a land: with death (the firstborn of Egypt, the camp of Assyria, Uzzah), with plague and disease, with blindness and madness, with blight on the crops, or by the sword of an enemy. He strikes to judge, and he strikes his own people to correct them; where they return, he heals.

evidence.note: “I will stretch out my hand and strike (וְהִכֵּיתִי) Egypt with all my wonders which I will do in its midst.”
“I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast”; done in Exo 12:29.
“I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with the pestilence (בַּדָּבֶר).”
“On the day of my striking (הַכֹּתִי) every firstborn in the land of Egypt I set apart for myself every firstborn in Israel.”
“To the striker of Egypt (לְמַכֵּה מִצְרַיִם) in their firstborn.”
After the flood: “I will not again strike (לְהַכּוֹת) every living thing, as I have done.”
The men at Lot's door “they struck with blindness (הִכּוּ בַּסַּנְוֵרִים)”; so Elisha's prayer, 2Ki 6:18.
“Yahweh struck the people a very great striking (מַכָּה רַבָּה מְאֹד)”, while the flesh was still between their teeth.
“I will strike it with the pestilence and dispossess it.”

“Yahweh will strike you (יַכְּכָה) with consumption and with fever and with inflammation … and with blight and with mildew”; with the boils of Egypt (Deu 28:27), with madness and blindness (Deu 28:28), on the knees and the legs (Deu 28:35).
“I also will strike you seven times for your sins.”
The hand of Yahweh was heavy on the men of Ashdod, “and he struck them with tumours”.
“God struck him (וַיַּכֵּהוּ) there for the error, and he died there beside the ark of God”: Uzzah.
“The angel of Yahweh went out and struck in the camp of Assyria a hundred and eighty-five thousand … all of them dead bodies.”
“An angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give God the glory”: Herod, in the words of 2Ki 19:35.
The anger of Yahweh burned against his people, “and he stretched out his hand against it and struck it”.
“I struck you with blight and with mildew … yet you did not return to me”; Hag 2:17.
“In vain I struck (הִכֵּיתִי) your sons; they did not take correction (מוּסָר)”: the blow was meant to correct.
“You struck them, but they did not feel pain … they refused to take correction … they refused to return.”
“The people did not return to the one striking it (הַמַּכֵּהוּ), and Yahweh of armies they did not seek.”
“Come, let us return to Yahweh; for he has torn and he will heal us, he struck (יַךְ) and he will bind us up.”
“For the iniquity of his gain I was angry and struck him … I have seen his ways, and I will heal him.”
To Zion: “in my wrath I struck you, and in my favour I have had compassion on you.”
“With the blow of an enemy (מַכַּת אוֹיֵב) I struck you, the correction of a cruel one, for the greatness of your iniquity.”
The adversary went out from before Yahweh “and struck Job with bad boils from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head”: the words of Deu 28:35.
“I will strike every horse with bewilderment and its rider with madness.”
Elijah is sent “lest I come and strike the land with a ban (חֵרֶם)”.
Of the shoot from the stock of Jesse: “he will strike (וְהִכָּה) the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will put the wicked to death.”
“Out of his mouth goes a sharp sword, that with it he should strike the nations”: Isa 11:4.
“Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man my fellow, declares Yahweh of armies: strike (הַךְ) the shepherd, and the flock will be scattered.”
Jesus on the night he was betrayed: “for it is written, I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered”; so Mrk 14:27. The striker is God.

senses.gloss: strike (a thing: rock, water, ground, building); of hail, sun, a worm: beat on, smite
senses.definition: To strike a thing with a staff, a cloak, an arrow or a weapon; and of hail, the sun or a worm, to beat on or attack what it harms.

evidence.note: “You shall strike (וְהִכִּיתָ) on the rock, and water will come out of it”; Moses struck the rock twice with his staff at Kadesh (Num 20:11); Psa 78:20.
He lifted the staff “and struck the water that was in the river”, and it turned to blood; so the dust of the ground (Exo 8:12–13).
Elijah rolled up his cloak “and struck the waters, and they were divided this way and that”; Elisha, 2Ki 2:14.
Elisha to Joash with the arrows: “Strike on the ground”; he struck three times and stopped.
“Strike the capital, and the thresholds will shake.”
Yahweh “will strike the great house into fragments”; Amo 3:15.
Saul sought “to strike with the spear into David and into the wall”, and “struck the spear into the wall”.
The priest's servant “struck (וְהִכָּה) into the pan” with the fork: thrust it in.
The he-goat “struck the ram and broke its two horns”.
“The hail struck (וַיַּךְ) in all the land of Egypt all that was in the field, from man to beast; and every plant of the field the hail struck.”
“By day the sun will not strike you, nor the moon by night”; Isa 49:10; Jon 4:8, where the sun struck on Jonah's head and he grew faint.
The worm “struck the plant, and it withered”.
Of Israel restored: “he will strike his roots (וְיַךְ שָׁרָשָׁיו) like Lebanon”: drive them in.

senses.gloss: clap (the hands); (of the heart) smite one
senses.definition: With כַּף, “palm”: to strike the hands together, in acclaim or in anger. With “heart” as subject: a man's heart strikes him when he knows he has done wrong.

evidence.note: At the crowning of Joash “they struck palm (וַיַּכּוּ־כָף) and said, May the king live!”
“Prophesy, and strike palm to palm”; and Yahweh: “I also will strike my palm to my palm, and I will rest my fury” (Ezk 21:22).
“Strike with your palm and stamp with your foot, and say, Alas!”
“I have struck my palm at your unjust gain.”
“The heart of David struck him (וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד אֹתוֹ), because he had cut off the skirt that was Saul's.”
“The heart of David struck him after he had numbered the people; and David said to Yahweh, I have sinned greatly.”

stems.gloss: be struck, beaten; be struck dead; be struck (by God, by plague); (of a city) be struck, fall

senses.gloss: be beaten; be struck dead; be wounded
senses.definition: The passive of the hiphil in its senses between men: to be beaten, to be wounded, to be struck dead.

evidence.note: “The officers of the sons of Israel were beaten (וַיֻּכּוּ)”; they tell Pharaoh, “your servants are beaten (מֻכִּים)” (Exo 5:16).
“If the thief is found breaking in, and is struck (וְהֻכָּה) and dies, there is no blood for him.”
“The name of the man of Israel who was struck (הַמֻּכֶּה), who was struck with the Midianitess, was Zimri”: killed by Phinehas' spear; so of Cozbi, Num 25:15, 18.
“Their young men struck of the sword (מֻכֵּי־חֶרֶב) in the battle.”
“What are these wounds (הַמַּכּוֹת) between your hands? … Those with which I was struck (הֻכֵּיתִי) in the house of my friends”: the verb and its noun together.

senses.gloss: be struck (by God: with disease, plague, judgment)
senses.definition: To be struck by God with disease or judgment; of a heart or a plant, to be blasted and wither. Of the servant of Yahweh, it is what men took him to be.

evidence.note: In Ekron “the men who did not die were struck (הֻכּוּ) with tumours”.
“On what will you be struck (תֻכּוּ) any more, that you add revolt? The whole head is sick”: the nation under Yahweh's blows, and none of the wounds bound up (Isa 1:6).
“Surely our sicknesses he bore … and we reckoned him plagued, struck of God (מֻכֵּה אֱלֹהִים), and afflicted.” The next verse corrects the reckoning: “but he was pierced for our transgressions.”
“Ephraim is struck (הֻכָּה); their root is dried up, they will bear no fruit.”
“My heart is struck like grass and withered.”

senses.gloss: (of a city) be struck, fall to an enemy
senses.definition: Of Jerusalem: to be struck by the enemy, that is, taken and its people slain.

evidence.note: The fugitive from Jerusalem came saying, “The city is struck (הֻכְּתָה הָעִיר).”
“In the fourteenth year after the city was struck.”

senses.gloss: be struck down
senses.definition: Once, of a man killed in battle.

evidence.note: David's letter about Uriah: set him where the fighting is fiercest and draw back from him, “וְנִכָּה וָמֵת, that he may be struck and die”.

senses.gloss: be struck down (by hail)
senses.definition: Twice, of standing crops beaten down by the hail in Egypt.

evidence.note: “The flax and the barley were struck (נֻכָּתָה), for the barley was in the ear and the flax in bud; but the wheat and the spelt were not struck (לֹא נֻכּוּ), for they are late.”

evidence.locator: Zec.13.7, הַךְ → πατάξατε; Exo.2.12, וַיַּךְ → πατάξας; Exo.12.12, וְהִכֵּיתִי → πατάξω; Isa.11.4, וְהִכָּה → πατάξει; 2Ki.19.35, וַיַּךְ → ἐπάταξεν; πατάσσω renders נָכָה ×248 and more in unlemmatised forms

evidence.note: Zec 13:7 quoted: “I will strike (πατάξω) the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.”
Exo 2:12: Moses “avenged the oppressed one, striking (πατάξας) the Egyptian”.
“An angel of the Lord struck (ἐπάταξεν) him”: as the angel of Yahweh struck the camp of Assyria.
The two witnesses have authority “to strike (πατάξαι) the earth with every plague (πληγῇ)”: the verb with its noun, as in the Hebrew of 1Sa 4:8.
Isa 11:4: “that with it he should strike (πατάσσῃ) the nations.”

evidence.locator: Num.22.28, הִכִּיתַנִי → πέπαικάς; Job.2.7, וַיַּךְ → ἔπαισεν; Lam.3.30, לְמַכֵּהוּ → παίοντι; 2Sa.6.7 → ἔπαισεν

evidence.note: “Prophesy to us, Christ: who is it that struck (παίσας) you?”; so Luk 22:64.

evidence.locator: Exo.2.11, מַכֶּה → τύπτοντα; Num.22.27, וַיַּךְ → ἔτυπτεν; 1Sa.17.36 → ἔτυπτεν

evidence.note: “To him who strikes (τύπτοντι) you on the cheek offer the other also”: Lam 3:30.
They took the reed and struck (ἔτυπτον) him on the head.
Paul to the high priest who ordered him struck: “God is about to strike (τύπτειν) you, whitewashed wall”; he appeals to the law, which has a man beaten only when he is judged guilty (Deu 25:1–2).

parallels.note: “Kill, slay”: striking and slaying in parallel lines.

evidence.note: “Has he struck him as with the striking of the one who struck him (הַכְּמַכַּת מַכֵּהוּ הִכָּהוּ)? Or is he slain as with the slaying of his slain?”
“Who struck many nations, and killed mighty kings.”

parallels.note: “Put to death” (hiphil of מוּת): beside or after הִכָּה, saying that the blow killed.

evidence.note: “He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will put the wicked to death.”

parallels.note: “Slay a man”: the law's name for the one who strikes a man dead.
“Devote to destruction”: the cities Joshua struck were devoted.

opposites.note: “Bind up”: Yahweh who struck binds up.
“Heal”: what Yahweh strikes he can heal, and what he strikes in judgment cannot be healed by others.

evidence.note: “Yahweh will strike you with the boils of Egypt … of which you cannot be healed.”

opposites.note: “Have compassion”: wrath struck, favour has compassion.

phrases.gloss: strike to the mouth of the sword: put to the sword
strike a soul: take a life
one who strikes a man so that he dies
strike a great striking: inflict a great slaughter
strike the palm: clap the hands
David's heart struck him: his conscience smote him

words.gloss: blow, stroke; wound; plague; slaughter, defeat
words.summary: The noun of the verb, with מ before the root and the נ lost in the doubled כ: the blow itself, and what the blow leaves. It is often the verb's own object (“struck them a great striking”). The plural is מַכּוֹת; 2Ki 8:29 and 9:15 have a plural מַכִּים. In 2Ch 2:9 Solomon promises Huram's woodcutters חִטִּים מַכּוֹת, where the parallel 1Ki 5:25 has “wheat, מַכֹּלֶת (food) for his house”; “beaten (threshed) wheat” is possible, but the link of that one use to the noun's sense is not clear.

senses.gloss: blow, stroke (of a rod, a whip, a sword)
senses.definition: A blow struck: the strokes of a judicial beating, a blow that corrects, the stroke of a sword.

evidence.note: “Forty he shall strike him, he shall not add, lest he add to strike him beyond these מַכָּה רַבָּה, many blows.”
“Bruises of a wound cleanse away evil, and מַכּוֹת, blows, the chambers of the belly.”
The Jews struck all their enemies מַכַּת־חֶרֶב, “a stroke of the sword, and killing and destruction”.
Babylon's king struck peoples in wrath מַכַּת בִּלְתִּי סָרָה, “a striking without ceasing”.

senses.gloss: wound
senses.definition: The wound a blow leaves on the body, which bleeds, is bound up and heals or does not; and, as a figure, the wound of a people or a city that Yahweh has struck.

evidence.note: Ahab, struck by an arrow between the joints of his armour, died at evening, “and the blood of the wound (דַּם־הַמַּכָּה) ran into the hollow of the chariot”.
Joram went back to Jezreel “to be healed of the wounds (הַמַּכִּים) with which the Arameans had struck him”; 2Ki 9:15.
“From the sole of the foot to the head there is no soundness in it: wound and bruise and fresh מַכָּה; they have not been pressed out or bound up or softened with oil.”
“What are these wounds between your hands?”
“Your breaking is incurable, your wound is grievous (נַחְלָה מַכָּתֵךְ)”; and the promise, “from your wounds I will heal you” (Jer 30:17).
“Why is my pain unending and my wound incurable, refusing to be healed?”
Samaria's “wounds are incurable; for it has come to Judah”.
To Nineveh: “there is no easing of your breaking; your wound is grievous.”
“In the day Yahweh binds up the breaking of his people, and heals the wound of his blow (מַחַץ מַכָּתוֹ)”: the blow was his, and so is the healing.

senses.gloss: plague, stroke (from God)
senses.definition: A blow from Yahweh on a people or a land: disease, disaster, the plagues of Egypt and the plagues of the covenant's curses. It stands beside “sickness” and is counted “seven times” for sins.

evidence.note: “If you walk contrary to me … I will add on you מַכָּה seven times, according to your sins.”
“Yahweh will make your plagues (מַכֹּתְךָ) extraordinary, and the plagues of your seed: great and lasting plagues, and bad and lasting sicknesses.”
“Every sickness and every plague (מַכָּה) that is not written in the book of this law.”
The generation to come will see “the plagues of that land, and its sicknesses with which Yahweh has made it sick”.
The Philistines: “these are the gods who struck (הַמַּכִּים) Egypt with every plague (בְּכָל־מַכָּה) in the wilderness.”
Everyone passing Jerusalem “will be appalled and hiss at all its plagues”; of Edom, Jer 49:17; of Babylon, Jer 50:13.
In Jerusalem “before me continually are sickness and מַכָּה”.
“To strike the earth with every plague (πάσῃ πληγῇ)”: the phrase of 1Sa 4:8.
“God will add to him the plagues that are written in this book”: Deu 28:61 and 29:20 turned about.

senses.gloss: slaughter, defeat
senses.definition: The striking down of men in battle or by Yahweh's hand: a slaughter, measured by the number who fell.

evidence.note: “He struck them מַכָּה־גְדוֹלָה at Gibeon”; Jos 10:20, “a very great striking, until they were finished”.
“הַמַּכָּה was very great: there fell of Israel thirty thousand footmen.”
“הַמַּכָּה הָרִאשֹׁנָה that Jonathan and his armour-bearer struck was about twenty men.”
The people mourned “because Yahweh had struck among the people a great מַכָּה”.
Samson “struck them leg on thigh, a great striking”.
“Abijah and his people struck them a great מַכָּה, and there fell slain of Israel five hundred thousand chosen men.”
Yahweh will raise a whip against Assyria “like the striking of Midian (כְּמַכַּת מִדְיָן) at the rock of Oreb”.

evidence.locator: Deu.25.3, מַכָּה → πληγάς; Deu.28.59, מַכּוֹת → πληγάς; Deu.28.61 → πληγήν; 1Sa.4.8 → πληγῇ; Isa.1.6 → πληγή; Jer.30.17 → πληγῆς; Zec.13.6 → πληγαί; πληγή renders מַכָּה ×34

evidence.note: “The plagues (πληγάς) that are written in this book”: Deu 28:61; 29:20–21.
“Seven angels having the seven last plagues, for in them the wrath of God is finished”: seven, as Lev 26:21.
“His deadly wound (πληγή) was healed”: a wound, as 1Ki 22:35.
The robbers “laid blows on him (πληγὰς ἐπιθέντες) and went away, leaving him half dead”.
The servant who did not know, “and did things worthy of blows (πληγῶν)”, will be beaten with few.
“When they had laid many blows on them”; the jailer “washed their stripes” (Act 16:33).
Paul: “in blows (πληγαῖς) beyond measure … of the Jews five times I received forty less one”: the forty of Deu 25:3, kept one short.

parallels.note: “Breaking, fracture”: the wound of a people beside its breaking.
“Wound”, with חַבּוּרָה “bruise”: the three words for bodily hurt together.

opposites.note: “Heal”: a wound is healed or is past healing.

phrases.gloss: a great striking: a great slaughter

words.summary: Three times, always in the construct נְכֵה before the part that is stricken: the feet, the spirit. The first is shown by its own verse to be lameness from an injury; the second is a figure from it. Proverbs has the like phrase רוּחַ נְכֵאָה, “a stricken spirit” (Pro 15:13; 17:22; 18:14), from the by-form נכא, which is filed apart.

senses.gloss: stricken in the feet, lame
senses.definition: Of Mephibosheth: crippled in both feet by a fall when he was five.

evidence.note: “Jonathan the son of Saul had a son נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם … his nurse took him up and fled, and as she hurried to flee he fell and became lame (וַיִּפָּסֵחַ).”
Ziba to David: “There is still a son of Jonathan, נְכֵה רַגְלָיִם.”

senses.gloss: stricken in spirit
senses.definition: Of the man Yahweh looks to: one whose spirit is struck down, set beside “humble” and “trembling at my word”.

evidence.note: “To this one I will look: to the humble and נְכֵה־רוּחַ, stricken of spirit, and trembling at my word.”

phrases.gloss: stricken of feet: lame in both feet

words.summary: Once, in the plural נֵכִים (Psa 35:15), of those who gathered against the psalmist when he stumbled. The form is of this root, but the verse does not fix whether they are “stricken ones” (cripples, wretches, as נְכֵה רַגְלַיִם) or “strikers”; its sense rests on this one use and on the sibling words.

senses.gloss: stricken ones (or strikers)
senses.definition: Men who gather against the afflicted psalmist and tear at him without ceasing: either the stricken, the lowest of men, or those who strike him.

evidence.note: “At my stumbling they rejoiced and gathered; נֵכִים gathered against me, and I did not know; they tore and did not cease.”

words.summary: One use only (Job 12:5), and that uncertain. The spelling is the same as נָכוֹן “fixed, ready” of the root כון, and the line reads well either way: contempt for calamity is “ready for those whose foot slips”, or is “a blow for those whose foot slips”. It is kept here as a possible noun of this root; nothing but this verse supports it. The other tokens counted under this key (Nacon, 2Sa 6:6; Jachin, 1Ki 7:21; 2Ch 3:17; Neh 11:10) are names filed here by spelling and belong to כון.

senses.gloss: a blow (or: ready)
senses.definition: What awaits the man whose foot slips, in the thought of the man at ease: a blow, a push; or, as the word of the root כון, “made ready”.

evidence.note: “For calamity there is contempt in the thought of the one at ease, נָכוֹן for those whose foot slips.”

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܢܟܐ (nkā), with final ā where the Hebrew writes ה: to hurt, harm. It is rare in the New Testament (three times in two verses) and has no sense of a blow of the hand; for “strike” the Peshitta uses ܡܚܐ (mḥā), as at Mat 26:31 (דֵּאמחֵא לרָעיָא, “I will strike the shepherd”). What it keeps of the root is the injury done.

stems.gloss: hurt, be harmful to, be opposed to

senses.gloss: be hurtful to, be opposed to
senses.definition: Of the flesh and the spirit: each desires what harms, that is, what is against, the other.

evidence.note: “The flesh desires a thing דּנָכֵא, that is hurtful, to the spirit, and the spirit desires a thing that is hurtful to the flesh, and the two are contrary one to the other.”

senses.gloss: be harmed, afflicted
senses.definition: Of the sick whom Jesus healed: those who had been harmed by evil.

evidence.note: Jesus of Nazareth “went about and healed those דֵּאתנכִיו, who had been harmed, by the evil one, because God was with him”: the harmed are healed, as the struck are in Hos 6:1.

cognates.gloss: inflicting injury on an enemy; slaying and wounding among the enemy; making great slaughter
cognates.note: The verbal noun of نَكَى “injure, slay and wound (an enemy)”. Its sense is that of הִכָּה in war and of מַכָּה “slaughter”: the Arabic keeps the root for what is done to an enemy, the Hebrew uses it for every blow.

evidence.note: “The inflicting injury upon an enemy: slaying and wounding among the enemy: or making much slaughter, or a great, or vehement, slaughter or wounding, among the enemy: the inflicting a routing and overthrow among the enemy.”

cognates.note: The passive side of the same root: to be the one struck down, as Hebrew הֻכָּה and נִכָּה.

evidence.note: “He (an enemy) was defeated, and overcome.”

cognates.gloss: peel the scab off a sore before it has healed; (dialect form of نَكَى) injure an enemy
cognates.note: The same root with hamza for its last letter, as Hebrew has נכא beside נכה. It is used of a sore made raw again, near to מַכָּה “wound”, and Lane gives it as a dialect form of نَكَى with “the enemy” as object.

evidence.note: “He peeled off the scab from the sore before it was healed, and it became moist in consequence. [See also نَكَى.] … نَكَأَ العَدُوَّ, and فِى العَدُوِّ, dial. form of نَكَى.”

cognates.gloss: (Jewish Aramaic) be injured, suffer; harm; deduct
cognates.note: Also written נְכָא. In the Jerusalem Talmud the ithpeel is “be injured, suffer harm” and the aphel “harm”, the sense the Peshitta's ܢܟܐ has; the pael “deduct” (take off a sum) is the later Hebrew piel נִכָּה. For “strike” the Targums use מְחָא, as the Peshitta does.

evidence.note: “Pa. to deduct … Ithpe. to be injured, suffer. Y. Ab. Zar. II, 41d top: the first drank and did not die, but were sick … let him cross, he shall not be injured … Af. to harm. Y. Sabb. III, 6a bot.: can he harm her in any manner?”

doctrine.statement: The law's phrase for killing is to “strike a soul”. “A man who strikes any soul of man shall surely be put to death; and one who strikes the soul of a beast shall make it good, soul for soul” (Lev 24:17–18). The manslayer is מַכֵּה־נֶפֶשׁ, “one who strikes a soul” (Num 35:11, 15, 30; Jos 20:3); the avenger of blood may “strike him, a soul” (Deu 19:6), and Reuben says of Joseph, “let us not strike him, a soul” (Gen 37:21). When Joshua took the cities, “they struck every soul that was in it to the mouth of the sword … nothing that breathed was left” (Jos 11:11; 10:28). In these verses the soul is what a blow of iron, stone or sword kills, in man and in beast alike. It follows that the נֶפֶשׁ is the living creature itself and its life, which dies when it is struck, and not a part of a man that outlives the blow.

Yahweh's servant says, “my back I gave to strikers” (Isa 50:6), and Micah, in the verse before the ruler from Bethlehem is named, “with the rod they strike on the cheek the judge of Israel” (Mic 4:14; 5:1). Those who watched him suffer “reckoned him plagued, struck of God, and afflicted” (Isa 53:4), as a man struck for his own sin; the prophet answers, “but he was pierced for our transgressions”, and yet also, “Yahweh was pleased to crush him” (Isa 53:5, 10). Zechariah gives Yahweh's own words: “Sword, awake against my shepherd, and against the man my fellow: strike the shepherd, and the flock will be scattered” (Zec 13:7). Jesus took this of himself on the night he was arrested, and quoted it with God as the striker: “I will strike the shepherd” (Mat 26:31; Mrk 14:27). That night and the next day men spat on him and struck him on the face and on the head with a reed (Mat 26:67–68; 27:30). The apostles say the same two things together: he was delivered up “by the determined counsel and foreknowledge of God”, and killed by the hands of lawless men, who did “whatever your hand and your counsel determined before to be done” (Act 2:23; 4:27–28). So from the verses: the one struck is a man (גֶּבֶר), Yahweh's shepherd and his fellow, and another than Yahweh, who commands the sword against him; his death was God's own purpose and not God's anger at his sin; and those who struck him were guilty of it all the same.

Yahweh says of Judah, “in vain I struck your sons; they did not take correction” (Jer 2:30), and Jeremiah, “you struck them, but they did not feel pain … they refused to return” (Jer 5:3); Isaiah, “the people did not return to the one striking it” (Isa 9:12); Amos and Haggai, “I struck you with blight and mildew, yet you did not return to me” (Amo 4:9; Hag 2:17). The law had said that the blows would be added “seven times” if Israel would not listen (Lev 26:21, 24). Where the blow is received, healing follows from the same hand: “he struck, and he will bind us up” (Hos 6:1); “I struck him … I have seen his ways, and I will heal him” (Isa 57:17–18); “with the blow of an enemy I struck you … from your wounds I will heal you” (Jer 30:14, 17); Yahweh “heals the wound of his blow” (Isa 30:26). A father does the same with the rod, and the son “will not die” (Pro 23:13–14). So Yahweh's striking of his own people is correction: its purpose is that they return, and it ends in healing for those who do.

Of the shoot from the stock of Jesse, on whom the spirit of Yahweh rests, Isaiah says: “he will judge the poor with righteousness … and he will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will put the wicked to death” (Isa 11:4); and then, “they will not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of Yahweh” (Isa 11:9). Revelation shows Jesus coming with a sharp sword out of his mouth, “that with it he should strike the nations, and he will shepherd them with a rod of iron” (Rev 19:15). Malachi ends with Elijah sent before the day of Yahweh, “lest I come and strike the land with a ban” (Mal 3:24). The place struck, and then filled with the knowledge of Yahweh, is the earth: the judgment at Christ's coming falls on the nations here, and his reign that follows is here.

When Noah came out of the ark Yahweh said, “I will not again strike every living thing, as I have done” (Gen 8:21). What he had done is told in the chapter before: “all flesh that moved on the earth expired … he wiped out every living thing that was on the face of the ground … only Noah was left, and those with him in the ark” (Gen 7:21, 23). The promise has meaning only if the flood struck every living thing on the land, and not the creatures of one region.

note: Root: נכה, the key the words are filed under; no other entry has it. Counts: the verb's key n.dk.aa counts 613 tokens, but 113 of them are “no stem” tokens filed here by spelling (בָהּ and the like, which belong to the preposition בְּ, and Hephzibah, Isa 62:4); the verb's own uses are about 500 (hiphil 481, hophal 16, pual 2, niphal 1). Five hiphil participles (הַמַּכִּים, 1Sa 4:8; 2Ki 14:5, 6; 2Ch 25:3; 28:23) are also counted under the noun's key n.dk.ae, and the noun's plural הַמַּכִּים in 2Ki 8:29; 9:15 under the verb's. The key n.dk.ad (נָכוֹן, 5 tokens) has one use in question, Job 12:5; the other four are the names Nacon and Jachin, which belong to כונ. The key m.bw.ao is a cross-reference with no tokens. Left out: נְכוֹ / נְכֹה, Pharaoh Neco (n.dk.af, 8 tokens; TIPNR Neco@2Ki.23.29), filed under this root by spelling only: it is the Egyptian king's name Nkꜣ.w (TLA lemma 861336), so it has no name entry here; if a name entry is wanted it should be an Egyptian loan under its own root. No personal name is formed from this root, so no name entries were drafted. For the reviewer: (1) Nacon (2Sa 6:6, TIPNR Nacon@2Sa.6.6), whose threshing floor is where “God struck” Uzzah (2Sa 6:7), is spelled as the niphal participle of כון and filed there; 1Ch 13:9 calls it Chidon; a play on הִכָּה is possible but nothing in the text says so. (2) The by-form נכא (נָכָא, נָכֵא, נְכָאִים: Isa 16:7; Pro 15:13; 17:22; 18:14; Job 30:8) has its own BDB key and is not treated here; it probably belongs in this entry as words with root נכא, as the Peshitta verb has been given. (3) Zec 13:6 (“wounds between your hands”) is cited only for the words; whether the speaker is the false prophet of 13:4–5 or the shepherd of 13:7 is not decided here, and it is not used in the doctrine. (4) נֵכִים (Psa 35:15) and נָכוֹן (Job 12:5) rest on one use each. (5) 2Ch 2:9 חִטִּים מַכּוֹת against 1Ki 5:25 מַכֹּלֶת. Leads not followed: Ge'ez nakaya “injure, hurt” (Leslau 1987; Dillmann 1865: locators not checked, so not cited); Old South Arabian nky (Biella 1982 scan not searched); Syriac ܢܟܝܢܐ “harm, injury” and the wider use of ܢܟܐ in the Old Testament Peshitta (Payne Smith 1903, page not checked); SEDRA files the Peshitta verb as lexeme 1963, NCA (root 1175), “harm; be opposed to”, with the word forms at Act 10:38 and Gal 5:17 (twice). The Septuagint also renders the verb by μαστιγόω where it is a flogging (Exo 5:14; Deu 25:2–3), which Heb 12:6 uses in quoting Pro 3:12, a verse without this root; not recorded as a rendering. The later Hebrew piel נִכָּה “deduct” is not scriptural.
